name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,289

clue.text: Reputedly boring individual teaches ceramicist

blocks.note: to teach someone a skill is to train them
a ceramicist makes pots, so is a potter

explanation.surface: A dull person gives lessons in pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'teaches' act on the ceramicist; it is really a synonym standing beside another synonym. The stereotype of the dull hobbyist noting locomotive numbers is British.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobbyist who logs locomotive numbers is the stock British stereotype of a tedious, obsessive person.

clue.text: Too lazy to work, Blondie beginning to eat bananas

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that single letter is kept
bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The singer from Blondie is too lazy to work and just starts eating bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: Blondie is the band (and its singer), but here it is just seven letters of fodder; 'bananas' looks like the food being eaten but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone utterly lazy, as idle as if right down to the bone, who will not lift a finger.

clue.text: Restore this section of permafrost ethically

indicators.note: a section is a slice cut from something longer, so the letters come from inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: An appeal to restore the frozen ground in an ethical way.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans permafroST ETHically. STET is the proofreader's instruction to keep a crossed-out word after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofreaders write this Latin word ('let it stand') in the margin to cancel a deletion, reinstating the original text.

clue.text: Ruin wild party pinching silver

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip something between the fingers, so one piece is held tightly inside another

blocks.note: a rave is a wild dance party
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A wild party is ruined when someone steals the silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' pretends to mean stealing, which suits the party guests; in the wordplay it means gripping, so one piece holds the metal's chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to damage something severely and destroy it, as an army or storm lays waste to land.

clue.text: Sweetheart delivered sufficient melon

indicators.note: a speech is delivered when spoken out, so what follows is heard rather than read

blocks.note: a common term of endearment
'due' as in due care: adequate, as much as is needed

explanation.surface: A lover hands over enough melon for everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' reads as handing something over; here it means spoken. DUE in the sense of adequate, as in 'with due care', sounds like DEW.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a variety of sweet melon with smooth pale rind and green flesh, a specific example of the fruit.

clue.text: Ascending sequence in Handel’s Imeneo is key

indicators.note: a sequence inside a longer run of text is a string of consecutive letters lifted from it
in a down entry, going upward means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the join, read backwards

explanation.surface: A musical commentator notes a rising run of notes in a Handel opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Musical words 'ascending sequence' and 'key' point to scales, but key is the definition. The letters handEL'S Imeneo read upwards give ISLE; the italics on the opera title are only styling.
explanation.definitionFit: A key (or cay) is a low small island, as in the Florida Keys, so it names a small piece of land in water.

clue.text: Australian native’s time to settle down

blocks.note: a roo is a kangaroo; the possessive supplies the S
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: It is bedtime for a kangaroo.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-S, which looks like grammar, contributes a letter: ROO'S + T.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds perch for the night on a branch, and people use the same verb loosely for settling in for the night.

clue.text: This suggests Laura’s excited to receive love

definitions.text: This suggests Laura’s excited to receive love

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up and agitated, so they get rearranged
to receive something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the name with its possessive S, taken as letters
love is zero in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A hint that Laura is thrilled because she is about to be loved.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read as wordplay, LAURA'S rearranged takes in O; read whole, it describes the state the answer names, with 'This' standing for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being excited at the prospect of receiving love is exactly the state of stimulation or excitement the noun describes.

clue.text: Changing sport, reply to office for recovery of kit

indicators.note: changing something alters its form, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: twelve letters of fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone switching sports writes to the office to get their old gear back.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'to' looks like it links reply and office, but it is fodder. In Britain the lost property office is where mislaid items are handed in and claimed (lost and found elsewhere).
explanation.definitionFit: A place where people reclaim belongings they have mislaid, such as sports gear left on a train, is the lost-and-found.

clue.text: I retain peculiar disinclination to move

indicators.note: peculiar means odd or strange, so the letters appear in an odd arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
six letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to a strange reluctance to get up and go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peculiar' seems to describe the disinclination but it acts on 'retain', the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The physics term for a body's tendency to stay at rest also means, in everyday use, a lazy unwillingness to act or change.

clue.text: Son follows description of six and eight irons?

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the first-named piece is placed at the end

blocks.note: both numbers are divisible by two
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A golfer's son follows him round, describing the six-iron and eight-iron.
explanation.walkthrough: Six and eight irons are golf clubs, which makes 'irons' look like a noun; the definition is the verb, as in irons out.
explanation.definitionFit: To iron a surface is to smooth it flat, and to even it is to make it level, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Item from bakery and fizzy water brought up for auditor

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so the word is taken as heard, not as spelt

blocks.note: soda water is carbonated water
a child brought up is raised, or bred

explanation.surface: A bakery item and a fizzy drink are served up for an accountant checking the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant, but it means a hearer. 'Brought up' looks like a reversal instruction; it is the definition of BRED.
explanation.definitionFit: This loaf, leavened with bicarbonate of soda instead of yeast, is a staple Irish baked product sold in bakeries.

clue.text: Bad breath surrounds old boy in loose clothing

indicators.note: something bad has gone wrong, so its letters are put out of order
to surround something is to enclose it, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil of a school

explanation.surface: An old man with bad breath lounges about in baggy clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad breath' reads as halitosis; 'Bad' is the anagram signal for 'breath'. The rearranged letters split around OB.
explanation.definitionFit: A robe worn before or after bathing is a garment tied loosely at the waist, hence loose-fitting wear.

clue.text: Friend coming round for drink

indicators.note: coming round means turning about, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: A friend drops by to have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming round' reads as visiting; it is the instruction to turn the friend backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals such as cats drink by scooping liquid up with the tongue, which is what this verb describes.

clue.text: Descend below ground, where cruise ends

indicators.note: in a down entry, something placed below sits lower, so the first-named piece comes second

blocks.note: land is ground, as opposed to sea
to fall is to descend

explanation.surface: An instruction to go down under the earth, placed where a voyage finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below ground' reads as underground, but 'below' only positions the pieces in this down entry, putting the verb under the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's arrival at the shore after a sea voyage is its landfall, the point where the journey reaches land.

clue.text: What encourages Sergio García? Endless holes

indicators.note: something without ends has lost both its first and last letters, keeping the middle

blocks.note: the word minus its outer letters

explanation.surface: What spurs on the Spanish golfer Sergio García? Hole after hole, forever.
explanation.walkthrough: Sergio García is a Spanish golfer, so 'holes' seems to belong to golf; it is the fodder, trimmed at both ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish crowds shout this cheer of approval, so a Spaniard would be urged on by it.

clue.text: Chopped up wood taken for one-on-one combat

indicators.note: chopping something up cuts it into bits that can be reassembled in any order

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Splintered wood is used in a fight between two people.
explanation.walkthrough: Chopping wood suits a martial art known for smashing boards, which is neat, but 'Chopped up' is only the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This Korean martial art is fought as a bout between two opponents, a form of unarmed duel.

clue.text: Some scores important having lost wicket

indicators.note: something that has lost a part no longer contains it, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: a weighty matter is an important one
W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a wicket

explanation.surface: A cricket report says some big innings mattered despite losing a wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'scores' mean runs; here a score is twenty, and four of them make the answer. Remove the W from the front of WEIGHTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is an old word for twenty, so four scores, a handful of them, make this number.

clue.text: Having returned, make strong argument against potato?

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: to rebut is to argue against and refute a claim

explanation.surface: Back again, someone makes a powerful case against the potato.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a potato is an example of the answer rather than a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A potato is a classic example of a swollen underground stem that stores food, the botanical type named by the answer.

clue.text: Scottish child, heartlessly, in outhouse

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is cut out

blocks.note: bairn is the Scots word for a child

explanation.surface: A Scottish child is cruelly kept in a shed.
explanation.walkthrough: The five-letter Scots word loses its middle letter, the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a farm building standing apart from the main house, used for storage or animals.

clue.text: Herbivore’s blunder eating skinned bird

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece is placed within the other
skinning removes the outer layer, so the first and last letters are stripped away

blocks.note: a gaffe is a social blunder
the word minus its outer letters

explanation.surface: A plant-eating animal makes the mistake of eating a plucked bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay. The joke is a herbivore eating meat.
explanation.definitionFit: This tall African animal browses on acacia leaves and eats only plants, so it is an example of a vegetarian creature.

clue.text: Raise seat

blocks.note: first meaning: to bring up children or animals
second meaning: the backside you sit on

explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like one instruction to lift a chair; they are separate meanings, a verb and a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for bringing up young and a noun for the buttocks, which are also called the seat.

clue.text: Unusual small portion is tasty snack

blocks.note: rare means unusual
a bit is a small piece

explanation.surface: An unusually small helping still makes a nice snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Welsh rarebit is melted cheese sauce on toast, a British savoury snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese on toast in its Welsh form is a light savoury dish eaten between meals, which is what the definition names.

clue.text: Assign everybody books

blocks.note: all means everybody
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: An instruction to hand out books to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Books' is a crossword convention for OT or NT, the two halves of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: To allocate or distribute a share to someone is to give it out, so the two verbs are synonyms.
